note.note:
Subjective:
- Presenting complaint and trigger/exposure:
  - Acute chest tightness for ~3 hours.
  - Recent upper respiratory infection last week (sore throat, runny nose); patient states current symptoms began after that illness.
- Symptom timeline and progression:
  - Chest tightness started ~3 hours prior to consultation.
  - Associated wheeze and persistent non-productive cough since the cold.
  - Shortness of breath mild, worse on exertion (walking upstairs); not short of breath at rest.
  - Cough slightly worse at night; overall symptoms have not resolved.
- ENT symptoms:
  - Recent sore throat and runny nose (last week); runny nose now improved.
  - Cough non-productive.
  - No reported throat closing/tightness of throat, no voice change/hoarseness, no dysphagia/odynophagia, no drooling.
  - No stridor or noisy breathing reported (wheeze only).
  - No facial, lip, tongue, or uvular swelling reported.
  - No current ear pain or neck swelling noted.
- Relevant past episodes and treatments:
  - History of asthma since childhood.
  - Prior severe asthma exacerbation in adolescence (age ~16–17) requiring hospital admission and intubation ("tube put down my throat"); stayed several days.
  - Usual asthma medications: Salbutamol (Ventolin) and Clenil Modulite (inhaled steroid).
  - Patient ran out of inhalers ~1 week ago while at university and has not had them for the past week.
- Allergies and current medications:
  - Allergies: dust (environmental). Childhood milk protein allergy. No known drug allergies.
  - Current/regular meds mentioned:
    - Salbutamol (Ventolin) — dose/route/frequency not documented; not currently available to patient.
    - Clenil Modulite (inhaled steroid) — dose/route/frequency not documented; not currently available to patient.
  - Prescriptions planned/mentioned:
    - Oral steroid tablets for 5 days, "two tablets in the morning" — specific steroid name and dose/route/frequency not documented.
    - Re-prescription of inhalers (Ventolin and Clenil) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
    - Spacer device to be supplied.
- Relevant social/contextual details:
  - Was away at university when inhalers ran out.
  - No other accompaniment stated.

Objective:
- Observable swelling/distribution: none reported.
- Airway/breathing descriptors:
  - Wheeze reported by patient.
  - Tight chest sensation; patient reports feeling unable to take a full breath at times.
  - Non-productive cough.
  - Mild exertional dyspnea (worse on stairs); not dyspneic at rest.
  - No stridor or noisy inspiratory breathing documented.
- Mental status/associated features:
  - No dizziness or syncope reported.
- Vitals and examination findings: Not recorded.
- Presence of another person with the patient: Not stated.

Assessment:
- Clinical impression: Acute asthma exacerbation (likely virus-triggered following recent upper respiratory infection) with chest tightness, wheeze and non-productive cough in a patient with known asthma and history of prior severe exacerbation requiring intubation.
- Key justifications:
  - Recent cold/URTI described by patient as preceding current symptoms.
  - Acute onset chest tightness and wheeze for ~3 hours.
  - Patient has been without maintenance and rescue inhalers for ~1 week.
  - Prior severe asthma requiring admission and intubation.
- Conflict noted:
  - Patient at one point stated "I'm doing pretty good, just on the Clenil and the Salbutamol," but earlier and elsewhere said he ran out of both inhalers a week ago and does not have them with him. (conflict noted)

Plan:
- Immediate actions taken/advised:
  - Doctor to send prescriptions for inhalers (Salbutamol/Ventolin and Clenil Modulite) — dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Oral steroid tablets prescribed for 5 days; regimen stated as "two tablets in the morning" — specific steroid name and dose/route/frequency not documented.
  - Spacer device will be supplied and instructions provided.
  - Prescription expected to be available to patient within approximately one hour (doctor stated this).
- Specific instructions given to patient:
  - Use Ventolin as needed; if using Ventolin more than every three hours, seek medical attention.
  - Rest and take time off work; doctor offered time off and noted patient can self-certify for the first seven days.
  - Read medication labels and be aware of steroid side effects; contact clinician if concerns.
  - Exact emergency/escalation instructions stated in the consult:
    - "If you should start to use the Ventolin more than... every three hours... at anytime, it's a good idea to seek medical attention."
    - "Any deterioration in your symptoms, like worsening shortness of breath... or feeling light-headed... then, seek further medical attention anytime please."
- Escalation criteria / red flags advised:
  - Increased or worsening shortness of breath.
  - Need to use salbutamol more frequently than every 3 hours.
  - New chest pain, light-headedness, or other clinical deterioration.
  - Any signs of airway compromise (throat/voice change, stridor) — seek urgent care (implied in warnings to seek immediate medical attention).
- Follow-up:
  - Obtain prescribed inhalers and spacer promptly.
  - If symptoms worsen despite medications, seek medical review/urgent care.
  - No formal ENT or allergy referral documented in the transcript.
  - No discussion of auto-injector or COVID-19 vaccine suitability recorded.

Quality checks / document_quality:
- Missing but clinically expected elements:
  - Objective observations: vital signs (respiratory rate, oxygen saturation, heart rate), physical examination findings (chest auscultation), peak expiratory flow measurement.
  - Specific names/doses/routes/frequencies for prescribed oral steroid and inhaler dosing.
  - Exact timing for follow-up clinical review or plan for escalation to ED.
  - Formal referral to asthma/allergy specialist or written asthma action plan.
  - Documentation of whether patient has a spacer available or demonstration of inhaler technique.
- Internal conflicts from transcript:
  - Conflicting statements about current inhaler use/availability: patient both stated he ran out of inhalers a week ago and later said he is "doing pretty good, just on the Clenil and the Salbutamol."
- Transcript quality:
  - Mostly clear; minor audio dropouts noted by doctor ("you were cutting in and out a little bit there") but sufficient for documentation.
